title: EMA Crossback
teaches: The EMA Crossback as we trade it: the first pullback into the rising short averages after a stock has turned up out of a decline (a Wedge Pop) or broken out, a hold day that reaches the zone and closes at or above the 20 EMA in the upper half of its range, the buy is the trade a few cents over the hold day's high within three sessions, the stop sits a few cents under the hold day's low, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

walkthroughs.title: UAA, June 2015: the clean stair-step
steps: UAA, 2015. A leader pops on 1.5x volume on 06-05, then drifts back to its averages in just 2 quiet sessions.
The hold day reaches the zone and closes above the 20 EMA, 9 still above 20. Nothing is bought yet.
2015-06-16: it trades over the hold day's high. Buy at market, 40.82. Stop a few cents under the hold day's low, 40.17.
Failure mode: the hold day's low breaks. Instead it reaches 3R in 5 days. Trim a third.

walkthroughs.title: CLS, October 2024: the undercut that held
steps: CLS, 2024. A pop on 1.1x volume on 09-19, then a quiet 4-day drift down to the averages.
The hold day undercuts the 20 EMA by 0.6% and closes back over it. That sits inside the zone.
2024-10-03: it trades over the hold day's high. Buy at market, 50.64. Stop 48.94, 3.4% away. A wider stop means fewer shares.
Failure mode: stopped within days. Instead 3R comes in 3 days. Trim a third.

walkthroughs.title: MU, August 2025: the clean crossback that failed
steps: MU, 2025. A pop on 08-08 on 1.3x volume, a 3-day drift, a hold day on 08-18. It looks clean.
2025-08-19: buy 123.70, stop 120.63. The size came from that stop, so the loss is already planned.
On 08-20 it trades down to 113.46 and takes the stop. We take the loss.
It reached 3R and 5R weeks later without us. A new buy needs a new hold day and a new trigger.

questions.q: What is the EMA Crossback?
choices: Any pullback in a long uptrend
A cross of the 9 under the 20 EMA
The first retest after a Wedge Pop
A gap down through the 200-day line
questions.answer: The first retest after a Wedge Pop
questions.why: The first retest after a Wedge Pop. Kell: it is the first time the stock retests its moving averages after a strong upward move.
questions.lesson_line: The crossback is the first pullback to the averages after the pop.

wrong.A cross of the 9 under the 20 EMA: That is the opposite. With the 9 under the 20 there is no reason to be long.
wrong.Any pullback in a long uptrend: Later pullbacks are other setups. The crossback is the first one after the pop.
wrong.A gap down through the 200-day line: A stock under the 200-day is not a long for us.

questions.q: A crossback holds the averages while the 9 EMA is still above the 20 EMA.
questions.why: True. The crossback is the pullback after the pop that holds the averages with the 9 still above the 20.
questions.lesson_line: Hold the averages with the 9 still over the 20.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We buy once price trades a few cents above the hold day's ___.
questions.why: High. The buy is at market once price trades a few cents above the hold day's high.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the trade over the hold day's high, not the touch.

questions.q: We buy the moment price touches the averages, before buyers show up.
questions.why: False. Buying the touch before buyers show is a named mistake. Kell says always wait for confirmation that buyers are stepping in.
questions.lesson_line: No hold day, no trigger, no buy. Wait for buyers.

questions.q: Where does the stop go on a crossback?
choices: Under the 200-day moving average
A few cents under the hold day's low
At the high made after the pop
Exactly on the hold day's low
questions.answer: A few cents under the hold day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the hold day's low. The stop comes first and the size comes from it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the hold day's low.

wrong.Under the 200-day moving average: That is far away and ignores the hold day's low.
wrong.Exactly on the hold day's low: A stop exactly on the low is hit by the first wiggle.
wrong.At the high made after the pop: That is above the buy. It would stop us out at once.

questions.q: With the 9 EMA under the 20 EMA, there is no reason to be long the stock.
questions.why: True. If the 9 EMA crosses under the 20 EMA, there is no reason to be long. Kell says the same of his 10 and 20-day lines.
questions.lesson_line: Fast average under the slow one: no long.

questions.q: In Kell's cycle, which stage comes right before the EMA Crossback?
choices: The Base n' Break
The Wedge Pop
The Exhaustion Extension
questions.why: The Wedge Pop. After the Wedge Pop, the stock often tests its moving averages again, known as the EMA Crossback.
questions.lesson_line: Pop first, crossback second.

wrong.The Exhaustion Extension: That comes late in the cycle, and a Wedge Drop follows it, not a crossback.
wrong.The Base n' Break: That is another pullback after the crossback, so it comes later.

questions.q: What does a Wedge Pop need besides crossing the averages?
choices: A strong price bar and volume
A gap down on light volume
Only a close above the 50-day
questions.answer: A strong price bar and volume
questions.why: A strong price bar and volume. Kell warns that the Wedge Pop is not simply about crossing the moving averages.
questions.lesson_line: A pop is price bars and volume, not just a cross.

wrong.Only a close above the 50-day: The pop is about the short averages, price bars and volume.
wrong.A gap down on light volume: That is weakness, not a pop.

questions.q: One close back over the 20 EMA is already a crossback.
questions.why: False. One close back over the 20 EMA is a pop setting up, not a crossback. The crossback is the pullback after the pop.
questions.lesson_line: A pop first. The crossback is the pullback that follows.

questions.q: What is the hold day?
choices: Reaches the zone, closes over the 20
The day of the pop
The day price first closes under the 20
questions.answer: Reaches the zone, closes over the 20
questions.why: A hold day reaches the zone. It closes at or above the 20 EMA in the upper half of its range.
questions.lesson_line: A hold day touches the zone and closes strong.

wrong.The day price first closes under the 20: That is a warning, not a hold.
wrong.The day of the pop: The pop comes first. The hold day is in the pullback.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The hold day closes at or above the ___ EMA.
questions.why: 20. The hold day closes at or above the 20-day EMA, in the upper half of its range.
questions.lesson_line: The hold day closes at or above the 20 EMA.

questions.q: A crossback can also follow a breakout, not only a Wedge Pop.
questions.why: True. A breakout over a base's pivot may stand in for the pop. Kell wrote of pulling back to the crossback after a nice breakout.
questions.lesson_line: Pop or breakout, then the first pullback.

questions.q: A clean crossback under the 200-day average is fine for us.
questions.why: False. The hold day closes above the 200-day, and a crossback gets no exception from the 200-day rule.
questions.lesson_line: No longs under the 200-day, crossback or not.

questions.q: What RS rating do we want on a crossback leader?
choices: 50, the middle of the market
80 or more
70, a decent stock
questions.why: 80 or more, in a strong group. A crossback is for leaders.
questions.lesson_line: Buy leaders: RS 80 or more in a strong group.

wrong.50, the middle of the market: A middling stock is not a leader.

questions.q: Bought at 116.55 with the stop at 112.39. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 129.03. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.

questions.q: Fill 116.55, stop 112.39. How far under the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 3.6. The stop sits 3.6% under the fill. Our stops usually sit within about 3%, so this one is wider.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent before you size the trade.

questions.q: Account 100,000, risk 0.5%, buy 116.55, stop 112.39. How many shares?
questions.why: 120. Divide the dollars at risk by the risk per share and round down. The shares come from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Shares come from the stop: dollars at risk divided by risk per share.

questions.q: A hold day's high is 64.00, its low 61.00 and its close 63.40. Where did it close in its range, in percent?
questions.why: 80. The close sits 80% of the way up the range, so it is in the upper half.
questions.lesson_line: A strong hold day closes in the upper half of its range.

questions.q: The 20 EMA is 100.00 and the hold day's low is 99.20. How far under the 20 EMA is the low, in percent?
questions.why: 0.8. The low sits 0.8% under the 20 EMA, inside the zone that runs down to about 1% under it.
questions.lesson_line: The zone reaches about 1% under the 20 EMA. Measure it.

questions.q: Keep the alert, or drop it?
choices: Lower the alert to Monday's close
Drop it; the setup is stale
Keep it; the high may still break
questions.answer: Drop it; the setup is stale
questions.why: Drop it. With no trigger within 3 sessions of the hold day, the setup is stale. Wait for a new hold day.
questions.lesson_line: Three sessions to trigger. After that, start over.

wrong.Keep it; the high may still break: The window has closed. A late break is a new decision.
wrong.Lower the alert to Monday's close: The trigger is the high, not the close.

questions.story: The hold day printed on Monday. By Thursday's close the stock has not traded over Monday's high.

questions.q: Buy tomorrow's break of the high?
choices: Yes; the hold day is clean
Yes, but only at half size
No; a report is too close
questions.answer: No; a report is too close
questions.why: No. No new buy if a report is due within 3 sessions. A clean hold day does not lift the rule.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date before every buy.

wrong.Yes; the hold day is clean: A report is a gap risk the chart cannot see.
wrong.Yes, but only at half size: The rule bars the new buy, not a size.

questions.story: The hold day closed today. The company reports in 3 sessions.

questions.q: Which name fits?
choices: EMA Crossback; the first retest
20 EMA Pullback; a tap of the 20
Wedge Pop; first close back over
questions.why: EMA Crossback. It is the first test of the averages after the stock closed back over them. A tap of a 20 EMA that has been rising for weeks is the 20 EMA Pullback.
questions.lesson_line: First test after the pop is the crossback. Later taps are pullbacks.

wrong.20 EMA Pullback; a tap of the 20: That is a tap of a 20 EMA that has been rising for weeks.
wrong.Wedge Pop; first close back over: The pop was eight sessions ago. This is the first pullback after it.

questions.story: The stock spent weeks under its averages, then closed back over the 9 and 20 EMA eight sessions ago. Now it tests those averages for the first time.

questions.q: Crossback or Wedge Pop?
choices: An EMA Crossback, after a dip
A Wedge Pop setting up today
A Base n' Break, a later rest
questions.answer: A Wedge Pop setting up today
questions.why: A Wedge Pop. One close back over the averages is a pop setting up, not a crossback. The crossback is the pullback after it.
questions.lesson_line: A first reclaim is the pop. The pullback after it is the crossback.

wrong.An EMA Crossback, after a dip: There has been no pullback yet. This is the reclaim itself.
wrong.A Base n' Break, a later rest: That is a later rest in the cycle.

questions.story: After weeks under its averages, a stock closes above both out of a tight range on 1.6x volume.

questions.q: Crossback or Base n' Break?
choices: EMA Crossback; the first rest
Base n' Break; a later rest
Wedge Pop; the move before
questions.answer: Base n' Break; a later rest
questions.why: Base n' Break. The crossback is the first rest after the pop. Kell's name for a later rest is the Base n' Break.
questions.lesson_line: First rest is the crossback. Later rests are Base n' Breaks.

wrong.EMA Crossback; the first rest: The crossback is the first rest. This is the second.
wrong.Wedge Pop; the move before: The pop was the move before the first rest.

questions.story: A stock popped, pulled into its averages once, and made a new high. Now it rests at the averages again.

questions.q: A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends the setup before the trigger.
questions.why: True. A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends it before the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy close under the 20 EMA ends the idea.

questions.q: Is this a crossback buy?
choices: No; the 9 is still under the 20
Yes, with a tighter stop
Yes; it is back over the 50-day
questions.answer: No; the 9 is still under the 20
questions.why: No. With the 9 EMA under the 20, there is no reason to be long. A crossback holds the rising 9 and 20 EMA with no run of closes under them.
questions.lesson_line: A stock that lost its averages is not a crossback.

wrong.Yes; it is back over the 50-day: Retaking the 50-day does not fix the short averages.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop: The stop does not repair a failed context.

questions.story: A stock closed under its 50-day for nine sessions. Today it closed back above it, but the 9 EMA is still under the 20.

questions.q: Crossback or bull flag?
choices: A bull flag
An EMA Crossback
A Wedge Pop
questions.why: A bull flag. The crossback's drift must reach the 9/20 zone and needs no pole. This drift never touched the averages.
questions.lesson_line: A crossback drift reaches the averages. A flag drift stays above them.

wrong.An EMA Crossback: The drift never reached the zone.
wrong.A Wedge Pop: A pop reclaims the averages after weeks under them.

questions.story: A stock jumps 32% in 12 sessions. Then it drifts tight for six sessions, well above the 9 and 20 EMA.

questions.q: What happens to the setup?
choices: Move the stop lower and wait
Buy anyway on the old trigger
Off until a new hold day forms
questions.answer: Off until a new hold day forms
questions.why: It is off. The hold day's low breaking before the trigger turns the setup off until a new hold day forms.
questions.lesson_line: Hold day's low breaks, setup off. Wait for a new hold day.

wrong.Buy anyway on the old trigger: The structure broke. The old trigger is gone.
wrong.Move the stop lower and wait: The stop never moves down or wider.

questions.story: Yesterday was the hold day. This morning, before any trigger, the stock trades under the hold day's low.

questions.q: What now?
choices: Buy the next day's high anyway
Wait one more day for the trigger
The setup is off
questions.why: The setup is off. A close under the 20 EMA on above-average volume ends it before the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A heavy close under the 20 EMA ends the idea.

wrong.Buy the next day's high anyway: The setup ended before any trigger.
wrong.Wait one more day for the trigger: The close under the 20 EMA on volume ends it.

questions.story: The hold day looked good. Then the stock closes under its 20 EMA on above-average volume.

questions.q: Kell's way of adding a second piece at the crossback is part of our plan.
questions.why: False. Our plan is one price with one stop: no pilot, no add on follow-through, no staggered stops. Adding or scaling in is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: We buy once at one price. Kell may add; we do not.

questions.q: What does our plan say?
choices: Add a second piece on the clear
Move the stop under the new low
No add; one price, one stop
questions.answer: No add; one price, one stop
questions.why: No add. A full new entry at one price with one stop: no pilot, no add on follow-through, no staggered stops. Adding or scaling in is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop. Kell may add; we do not.

wrong.Add a second piece on the clear: That is Kell's way, not our plan.
wrong.Move the stop under the new low: The stop only moves up on the plan's own steps.

questions.story: You bought the crossback over the hold day's high at 50.64. Two days later it clears the pop high.

questions.q: Is it a crossback?
choices: No; a Wedge Drop is next
Yes, buy the touch
Yes, it is the first pullback
questions.answer: No; a Wedge Drop is next
questions.why: No. After an Exhaustion Extension the next stage in Kell's cycle is a Wedge Drop, not a crossback.
questions.lesson_line: After a climax, the next stage is a drop, not a crossback.

wrong.Yes, it is the first pullback: The climax came first. The cycle is turning down.
wrong.Yes, buy the touch: Buying the touch is a named mistake.

questions.story: A stock ran far above its 10-day average in a climax and then rolled over. It now pulls back into its averages.

questions.q: Buy?
choices: No; it is under the 200-day
Yes, at half size with a stop
Yes; it is a textbook crossback
questions.why: No. The hold day must close above the 200-day, and a crossback gets no exception from the rule.
questions.lesson_line: A textbook shape under the 200-day is still a pass.

wrong.Yes; it is a textbook crossback: Shape does not lift the 200-day rule.
wrong.Yes, at half size with a stop: Size does not fix a failed gate.

questions.story: A textbook first crossback follows a gap-up Wedge Pop. The stock is still 6% under its 200-day.

questions.q: How does the market cue grade it?
choices: Higher; the stock is a leader
Lower; these fail most
The same; the index never matters
questions.why: Lower. Crossbacks taken with the Nasdaq under its 20 EMA fail most. The index cue lowers the grade, and the stop is still the exit.
questions.lesson_line: Watch the index. Crossbacks fail most with the Nasdaq under its 20 EMA.

wrong.Higher; the stock is a leader: A leader does not cancel a weak index.
wrong.The same; the index never matters: Kell trades smaller or stands aside during index corrections.

questions.story: AAPL had a clean crossback. The Nasdaq 100 had closed under its own 20-day EMA the day before the entry.

questions.q: Take it?
choices: Take it at full size anyway
Pass; Orange buys A+ only
Take it at half size instead
questions.why: Pass. Orange buys A+ only, and this one grades B.
questions.lesson_line: Orange: A+ only. A B grade waits.

wrong.Take it at half size instead: Orange allows A+ only, at any size.

questions.story: The market reading is Orange. A leader makes a clean crossback that you grade B.

questions.q: Is it a valid hold day?
choices: No; a weak close
Yes; the low reached the zone
Yes; it later reached 3R
questions.why: No. The hold day closed in the lower 3% of its range, not the upper half. The low reached the zone but the close gave it back.
questions.lesson_line: A hold day needs a strong close, not just a touch.

wrong.Yes; the low reached the zone: The close matters as much as the low.
wrong.Yes; it later reached 3R: That was luck, not the setup.

questions.story: GE touched the zone, but the hold day closed in the lower 3% of its range.

questions.q: Which gate fails?
choices: The close was too weak to hold
The low went too far under the 20 EMA
The 9 EMA crossed under the 20 EMA
questions.answer: The low went too far under the 20 EMA
questions.why: The depth. The hold day's low sat 2.1% under the 20 EMA, and the zone runs down to about 1% under it. A deeper undercut is a different shape.
questions.lesson_line: The zone ends about 1% under the 20 EMA.

wrong.The close was too weak to hold: The close was fine. The low went too deep.
wrong.The 9 EMA crossed under the 20 EMA: Nothing in the story says the averages crossed.

questions.story: AMAT's hold day closed back over the 20 EMA, but its low sat 2.1% under the line.

questions.q: Most crossbacks in our scan reached 3R before the stop.
questions.why: False. 28.9% reached 3R before the stop, and 82.6% hit the stop at some point. It is a probability trade.
questions.lesson_line: Most crossbacks stop out first. Size from the stop.

questions.q: How do you handle the size?
choices: Pull the stop in to 3% to fit
Use the 200-day line as the stop
Fewer shares; stop stays honest
questions.why: Fewer shares. The size comes from the stop, so a wider stop means fewer shares. Never tighten the stop to fit.
questions.lesson_line: A wide stop gets a smaller size, never a tighter stop.

wrong.Pull the stop in to 3% to fit: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap.
wrong.Use the 200-day line as the stop: That is far away and ignores the hold day's low.

questions.story: CLS: fill 50.64, honest stop 48.94, which is 3.4% away. Your risk budget is fixed.

questions.q: How do you respond?
choices: Take the loss; wait for a new trigger
Buy again at once; it looked so clean
Move the stop lower and give it room
questions.answer: Take the loss; wait for a new trigger
questions.why: Take the loss. After a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger as a new trade. MU later reached 3R and 5R without us, and the stop was still right.
questions.lesson_line: A clean setup can lose. Re-buy only on a new hold day and trigger.

wrong.Buy again at once; it looked so clean: A re-buy needs a new hold day, a new trigger and every rule.
wrong.Move the stop lower and give it room: The stop never moves down or wider.

questions.story: MU looked clean: a pop, a 3-day drift, a hold day. The next session it fell through the stop.

questions.q: On one stock we take at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.why: True. At most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. Each new try needs a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Cap the tries. A new try needs a new trigger.

questions.q: Which average is the default trail for a fast-moving crossback?
choices: The 10-day
The 50-day
The 200-day
questions.why: The 10-day for a fast mover, sold on a close below it. A steadier stock can use the 21-day.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover: trail the 10-day. Steadier: trail the 21-day.

wrong.The 50-day: Too slow for a fast mover.

questions.q: What is the plan?
choices: Add more while it is quiet
Sell it and free the money
Hold; the hold day was clean
questions.answer: Sell it and free the money
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
questions.lesson_line: A trade that does nothing for 10 days is sold.

wrong.Hold; the hold day was clean: The time stop does not care about the hold day.

questions.story: You bought a crossback 10 trading days ago. It has drifted sideways and is up only 0.6R.

questions.q: When do you take the first third?
choices: Sell the whole position
Wait for a higher price
At the open
questions.why: At the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past your trim level means trim at the open.

wrong.Wait for a higher price: The rule says take it at the open.
wrong.Sell the whole position: We trim a third and trail the rest.

questions.story: You bought at 116.55 with the stop at 112.39. Next morning the stock opens at 130.00, above 3R at 129.03.

questions.q: What governs the exit?
choices: First 30-minute low; out past 2R
Hold; wait for it to recover fully
Keep the old stop at 120.63
questions.why: The first 30-minute low is the new stop, and past 2R we get out. Here the loss is far past 2R.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop gets the 30-minute rule. Past 2R, get out.

wrong.Hold; wait for it to recover fully: The gap rule does not wait.
wrong.Keep the old stop at 120.63: The stock is already through it.

questions.story: You bought at 123.70 with the stop at 120.63, so 1R is 3.07. The stock gaps down and the first 30-minute low is 113.46.

questions.q: How do you play this one?
choices: Skip it; two sessions is too short
Buy at market, stop under hold low
Wait for a close over the hold high
questions.answer: Buy at market, stop under hold low
questions.why: Buy at market, 40.82, with the stop a few cents under the hold day's low, 40.17. It reached 3R in 5 days.
questions.lesson_line: Hold day, then the trade over its high, then the stop under its low.

wrong.Wait for a close over the hold high: We buy the trade through, at market.
wrong.Skip it; two sessions is too short: A quiet two-session pullback was the clean case.

questions.story: A leader popped on 1.5x volume. After two quiet sessions of pullback, the hold day closes above the 20 EMA. Next day it trades over the hold day's high.

questions.q: Is it a valid hold day?
choices: No; any low under the 20 EMA fails
No; the stop would be too wide
Yes; the undercut closed back over
questions.answer: Yes; the undercut closed back over
questions.why: Yes. The low undercut the 20 EMA by 0.6%, inside the zone, and the close came back over it.
questions.lesson_line: A small undercut that closes back over the 20 EMA still holds.

wrong.No; any low under the 20 EMA fails: The zone runs down to about 1% under the line.
wrong.No; the stop would be too wide: A wider stop means fewer shares. It does not void the setup.

questions.story: CLS drifted four quiet sessions. The hold day's low sat 0.6% under the 20 EMA, and it closed back over the line.

questions.q: Does a low exactly on the 20 EMA count?
choices: No; it needs a gap down
Yes; the low reached the zone
No; it must dip under the line
questions.answer: Yes; the low reached the zone
questions.why: Yes. The low only has to reach the zone, and the close is a strong one. ALGN drifted six sessions with its low exactly on the 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: The low reaching the 20 EMA is enough. The close does the rest.

wrong.No; it must dip under the line: The zone is a range. Reaching the line is enough.
wrong.No; it needs a gap down: A drift is the best case, not a gap.

questions.story: ALGN popped on an earnings gap. It drifted six sessions, the hold day's low sat exactly on the 20 EMA, and it closed strong.

questions.q: What warning did it carry?
choices: It came late in its own run
The 9 had crossed under the 20
The hold day had thin volume
questions.answer: It came late in its own run
questions.why: It was late in the stock's own advance, sixteen sessions after the pop. Late crossbacks fail most. LLY was stopped the next day.
questions.lesson_line: A long wait after the pop is a warning, not a gate. The stop still decides.

wrong.The hold day had thin volume: Nothing in the story says so.
wrong.The 9 had crossed under the 20: Nothing in the story says so.

questions.story: LLY gave a crossback sixteen sessions after its pop, after a long advance. The next day it hit the stop.

questions.q: Did that entry break the earnings rule?
choices: Yes; any report nearby is a no
Yes; it should have been held through
No; the report was 5 sessions away
questions.answer: No; the report was 5 sessions away
questions.why: No. The entry was five sessions before the report, outside the 3-session window. The stock still could not hold, and the stop did its job.
questions.lesson_line: Outside 3 sessions is legal. The stop is still the exit.

wrong.Yes; any report nearby is a no: The rule is a window of 3 sessions.
wrong.Yes; it should have been held through: We hold through a report only when up 5R.

questions.story: NFLX gave a crossback with the report's reaction day five sessions after the entry. The next day it hit the stop.

questions.q: Which entry is this?
choices: A Wedge Pop
The EMA Crossback
A Base n' Break, graded lower
questions.answer: A Base n' Break, graded lower
questions.why: A Base n' Break, graded lower. It was the second pullback into the zone since the pop, so it is not this card's entry, even though it worked.
questions.lesson_line: A winner can still be the wrong card. Count the rests.

wrong.The EMA Crossback: The crossback is the first rest. This was the second.

questions.story: AMZN popped on 10-30. It pulled into its averages on 11-21 for the second time since the pop and then ran 9.94R.

questions.q: What do you do with it?
choices: Ignore it; only the stock matters
Skip it; the index is a hard gate
Treat the index cue as a grade cue
questions.answer: Treat the index cue as a grade cue
questions.why: Treat it as a grade cue, not a gate. Kell sizes down or stands aside during index corrections, and a market Wedge Pop is the best cue.
questions.lesson_line: The index cue is a cue. A weak index lowers the grade.

wrong.Skip it; the index is a hard gate: The card calls it a cue, not a gate.
wrong.Ignore it; only the stock matters: A weak index makes crossbacks fail more often.

questions.story: A clean crossback sets up on a leader while the Nasdaq sits just under its 20-day EMA.

questions.q: Where does the stop go?
choices: Same stop: the hold day's low
At breakeven the moment you buy
Just under the 200-day average
questions.answer: Same stop: the hold day's low
questions.why: The same. The advanced version buys an intraday trigger on the hold day itself, with the same stop, the day's low.
questions.lesson_line: An earlier entry keeps the same stop. It does not widen it.

wrong.Just under the 200-day average: That ignores the hold day's low.
wrong.At breakeven the moment you buy: Breakeven comes at the first trim.

questions.story: On the hold day itself, the stock breaks its 65-minute high and you buy the advanced version.

questions.q: Buy at market?
choices: Yes, with a wider stop
No; more than 4% over the trigger
Yes; heavy volume confirms it
questions.answer: No; more than 4% over the trigger
questions.why: No. Skip if the fill is more than 4% above the trigger. Kell found even 3-4% above the averages was too much.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4% over the trigger you are chasing. Wait for the next hold day.

wrong.Yes; heavy volume confirms it: Volume does not lift the 4% limit.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop: Widening the stop is never the fix.

questions.story: The trigger was 50.64. The next time you look, the stock trades at 52.90 on heavy volume.

questions.q: Take the new hold day?
choices: Yes; the new hold day is a new trade
No; three tries this week are used
Yes, at half size
questions.answer: No; three tries this week are used
questions.why: No. At most 3 tries a week on one stock, and a new try needs a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week on one stock, six a month. Then stop.

wrong.Yes, at half size: Size is not the fix for a try limit.

questions.story: You have bought this stock three times this week, and each try stopped out. A fresh hold day just printed.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Take it at half size
Take it; the pattern is clean
Pass; it is too thin and too cheap
questions.answer: Pass; it is too thin and too cheap
questions.why: Pass. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
questions.lesson_line: The chart comes after the floor.

wrong.Take it at half size: Size does not fix a liquidity failure.
wrong.Take it; the pattern is clean: Thin names are not even watched.

questions.story: A neat crossback sets up on an 8 dollar stock that trades about 5 million dollars a day.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Pass; not a leader by our rule
Take it; 72 is close enough to 80
Take it at half size for now
questions.answer: Pass; not a leader by our rule
questions.why: Pass. We buy leaders, with an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group. An RS of 72 is not that.
questions.lesson_line: Buy leaders. A neat chart on a laggard waits.

wrong.Take it at half size for now: Size does not fix a leadership gap.

questions.story: A clean crossback sets up in a stock with an RS rating of 72.

questions.q: What is your call?
choices: Buy it; the stock is strong
Pass; Red means mostly cash
Buy a starter
questions.why: Pass. In a Red market we hold mostly cash.
questions.lesson_line: A great setup in a Red market waits.

wrong.Buy a starter: A starter in a Red market is still a long.
wrong.Buy it; the stock is strong: A strong stock does not cancel a Red market.

questions.story: A textbook crossback sets up on a leader. The market reading is Red.

questions.q: How does that history affect the grade?
choices: It lowers the grade
It raises the grade; it is due
It does not matter
questions.why: It lowers the grade. A stock whose crossbacks keep failing is a grade cue, and so are many crossbacks failing on low volume across the market.
questions.lesson_line: A stock with a history of failed crossbacks gets a lower grade.

wrong.It raises the grade; it is due: Past failures are a warning, not a reason to expect a win.

questions.story: A clean crossback sets up in a stock whose last three crossbacks all failed.

questions.q: Which crossback grades higher?
choices: They grade the same
The first one, after the gap-up pop
Crossback B, because it waited
questions.answer: The first one, after the gap-up pop
questions.why: The first one. A crossback after a powerful pop, a gap on heavy volume, is the A+ picture. Late crossbacks fail most.
questions.lesson_line: A strong pop and a short wait make the best crossback.

wrong.Crossback B, because it waited: A long wait makes the crossback late.
wrong.They grade the same: The pop and the timing matter.

questions.story: Crossback A comes 5 sessions after a gap-up pop on 3.6x volume. Crossback B comes 18 sessions after a 1.0x pop, with the stock already up 15% on the quarter.

questions.q: The best crossbacks come with the 200-day falling.
questions.why: False. We prefer the 200-day rising, as a grade cue. The best case is a fresh turn above a rising 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A rising 200-day is a grade cue.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the hold day just closed. Does it close in the upper half above the 20 EMA? Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; there was no gap
Take it; a strong hold day
Pass; two sessions is too short
questions.answer: Take it; a strong hold day
questions.why: Take it. The pop came on 1.5x volume, two quiet sessions of pullback, and the hold day closed above the 20 EMA. The trigger came the next day and reached 3R in 5 days.
questions.lesson_line: Check the close before the trigger: upper half, over the 20 EMA.

wrong.Pass; two sessions is too short: A quiet two-session pullback was the clean case.
wrong.Pass; there was no gap: A gap helps the grade. It is not required.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, a hold day just closed. Did it close in the upper half of its range? Take it or pass.
choices: Pass; it closed near the low
Take it; the low reached the zone
Take it; the 200-day is rising
questions.answer: Pass; it closed near the low
questions.why: Pass. The hold day closed in the lower 3% of its range, not the upper half. It still reached 3R, which is luck, not the setup.
questions.lesson_line: A touch of the zone is not enough. The close must be strong.

wrong.Take it; the low reached the zone: The close matters as much as the low.
wrong.Take it; the 200-day is rising: Context is fine. The hold day is the problem.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Buy half and set a stop later
Buy now before it runs away
Check the hold day and stop
questions.answer: Check the hold day and stop
questions.why: Check it yourself. Never take a trade from an alert, a post or a video without your own entry, stop and size.
questions.lesson_line: Someone else's alert is not a plan. Build your own entry, stop and size.

wrong.Buy now before it runs away: A buy with no stop and no size is a gamble.
wrong.Buy half and set a stop later: Half a gamble is still a gamble.

questions.story: A post says a stock is on its EMA Crossback right now. You have not looked at its hold day, stop or size.

questions.q: What is your call?
choices: Take it with a tighter stop
Pass; the 9 slipped under the 20
Take it; the hold day is strong
questions.why: Pass. With the 9 EMA under the 20, there is no reason to be long, even if the hold day closes strong.
questions.lesson_line: A strong hold day does not repair crossed averages.

wrong.Take it; the hold day is strong: A strong close does not fix the averages.
wrong.Take it with a tighter stop: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap.

questions.story: A leader above its 200-day pops, then pulls back. During the pullback the 9 EMA slips under the 20. The hold day closes strong.

questions.q: What does it tell you about the market?
choices: Buy more; they are cheap now
Be careful; risk appetite is weak
Nothing; each stock stands alone
questions.answer: Be careful; risk appetite is weak
questions.why: Be careful. Many crossbacks triggering and failing on low volume is a sign of weak risk appetite, and a cue to grade lower.
questions.lesson_line: When crossbacks keep failing around the market, grade lower.

wrong.Buy more; they are cheap now: Failures around the market are a warning, not a bargain.
wrong.Nothing; each stock stands alone: The market's pattern is part of the context.

questions.story: Over two weeks, many crossbacks across the market trigger and fail on low volume.

questions.q: What do you do about the stop?
choices: Keep the honest stop; cut size or skip
Pull the stop in to fit
Widen the stop
questions.answer: Keep the honest stop; cut size or skip
questions.why: Keep the honest stop. If it does not fit the risk, cut the size or skip. The stop only moves up, never wider.
questions.lesson_line: The stop does not bend to fit the size. The size bends to the stop.

wrong.Widen the stop: The stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Pull the stop in to fit: Pulling the stop in to fit the size is a trap.

questions.story: The honest stop is wider than your risk budget allows. A friend says to give it more room.

questions.q: Which pullback is the better crossback?
choices: Neither; both are the same
The slow, tight drift
The hard drop; it hit the zone faster
questions.why: The slow drift. Kell says the crossback works best when price gently moves sideways and the averages rise to meet it. TraderLion adds that a slow drift is ideal.
questions.lesson_line: Let the averages rise to price. A gentle drift beats a violent drop.

wrong.The hard drop; it hit the zone faster: Speed is not the point. The averages need time to rise.
wrong.Neither; both are the same: The cleaner and shallower pullback is better.

questions.story: Two stocks pop and then pull back to their averages. One drifts sideways for five sessions. The other drops hard in two.

questions.q: We buy a crossback with a market order the moment the trigger trades, in regular hours.
questions.why: True. Entries are market orders, placed as soon as price trades over the trigger, and only in regular hours.
questions.lesson_line: Market order at the trigger, regular hours only.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: It is 8:10 am, before the open. A thin pre-market print takes the stock a few cents over the hold day's high.
choices: Wait; market buy in regular hours
Buy at market now, before it runs away
Rest a limit order at the high now
questions.answer: Wait; market buy in regular hours
questions.why: Wait. No new buys outside regular hours, and entries are market orders. If the trigger trades after the open, buy then.
questions.lesson_line: A pre-market print is not your trigger. Regular hours only.

wrong.Buy at market now, before it runs away: Pre-market is outside regular hours. The rule is no new buys there.
wrong.Rest a limit order at the high now: Entries are market orders, bought in regular hours. A resting order is not our entry.

questions.q: A crossback trigger gaps and would fill at 54.60. The 10-day average is 49.00. How far above it, in percent?
questions.why: 11.4%. That is more than 10% above the 10-day average, so we skip it: too stretched to buy.
questions.lesson_line: More than 10% over the 10-day is a chase. Skip it.

questions.q: The fill is inside the 4% chase limit. Which rule says skip?
questions.story: The hold day's high was 100.00 and the 10-day average is 91.00. The stock opens next morning at 101.50, so a market buy fills near there.
choices: The 10% stretch rule
The 4% chase limit
The 1% volume ceiling
questions.why: The 10% stretch rule. A long more than 10% above its 10-day average is too stretched. 101.50 is more than 10% above 91.00.
questions.lesson_line: Two checks at the fill: distance from the trigger and distance from the 10-day.

wrong.The 4% chase limit: The fill is a little over the trigger, so the chase limit passes. The stretch rule is the one that fails.
wrong.The 1% volume ceiling: That caps the share count. Nothing here says the count is too big.

questions.q: A crossback stock trades 4,000,000 shares a day on average. What is the most shares our volume rule lets us hold?
questions.why: 40,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, whatever the risk math allows.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the average daily volume is the ceiling.

questions.q: Even on a textbook crossback, we never own more than 1% of the stock's average daily volume.
questions.why: True. The ceiling is 1% of average daily volume, and illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: A clean chart does not lift the volume ceiling.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Every position has a real stop order with the ___, not a stop kept in your head.
questions.why: Broker. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.

questions.q: Once the crossback stop is set, it only moves up. The one exception is the gap rule.
questions.why: True. The stop is the exit and it only moves up, never down or wider. The gap rule is the one exception.
questions.lesson_line: Set the stop before the buy. It only goes up from there.

questions.q: We pass on a clean crossback when the latest sales and earnings are not growing.
questions.why: False. Growing sales and earnings are preferred, but the chart comes first.
questions.lesson_line: Growth helps the grade. The chart still decides.

questions.q: Bought at 40.82, stop 40.17. At what price may the stop first go to breakeven?
questions.why: 42.12. Breakeven comes once the trade reaches 2R: the fill plus two times the distance to the stop. The rule runs from 2R to 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R. From 2R the stop can move up to your entry.

questions.q: From which R can the crossback stop go to breakeven?
choices: From 2R, at the first trim
From 1R, as soon as it moves up
Only at 5R, and not any sooner
From the first higher daily close
questions.why: From 2R, at the first trim by default. The rule allows 2R to 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, not before.

wrong.From 1R, as soon as it moves up: Too soon. The rule starts at 2R.
wrong.Only at 5R, and not any sooner: 5R is the far end of the range, not the only point. The rule allows 2R to 5R.
wrong.From the first higher daily close: A close is not a measure of R. The move is set in R, from 2R.

questions.q: You hold 120 shares. A third comes off at 3R and another third at 5R. How many shares sell at 5R?
questions.why: 40 shares. A third of 120 comes off at 3R, another third at 5R, then you trail the last third.
questions.lesson_line: Thirds: one at 3R, one at 5R, and the last rides the trail.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After the first third at 3R, another third comes off at ___, then you trail the rest.
questions.why: 5R. The second third comes off at 5R, and the last third rides the trail.
questions.lesson_line: 3R for the first third, 5R for the second, then trail.

questions.q: What is the move on your long?
questions.story: Your crossback winner has run four days straight, gapping up each morning, now far above its 10-day average.
choices: Sell a big part into the burst
Add a third piece into strength
Hold all of it and trail the 10-day
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run far above the 10-day on your own long is a judgment call, and we sell into strength.
questions.lesson_line: A climax run is a place to sell a big part, not to add.

wrong.Add a third piece into strength: We buy one price with one stop and never add. A burst is a place to sell.
wrong.Hold all of it and trail the 10-day: The trail is for the rest. Into a climax run we sell a big part first.
